sn36.21:1.2: Moḷiyasīvaka also appears in [an6.47](), where he also goes for refuge.
sn36.21:1.4: Sīvaka is referring to the Jains.
sn36.21:1.5: The view that all experiences are caused by past kamma is consistently rejected in the Suttas. This is reflected in the later Theravada commentaries, which describe five interacting _niyāmas_, or systems of natural law: seasons (_utu_), genetics (_bīja_), moral or immoral deeds (_kamma_), mind (_citta_), and principles of the teaching (_dhamma_). Nonetheless, the view that all experiences are caused by kamma is extremely common among modern Buddhists, and is often heard even from learned scholars. This is a harmful misunderstanding, as it has led to discrimination against the poor and disabled in Buddhist countries. One point of confusion is that rebirth into a particular life is caused by kamma, so in that general sense, kamma is a necessary condition for having a life in which one can experience anything. But the feelings experienced in that life are caused by a variety of things, not necessarily by kamma. | Note the use of _purisapuggala_ (“individual person”) as a Jain idiom. See [mn35:10.7]() and note, and [sn22.22]() and notes.
